headline: SpaceX Catches Falling Skyscraper, Declares Parallel Parking Solved
subheadline: *A day after mounting the cosmic kerb, the 20-storey booster slotted itself into the world's most aggressive cutlery drawer.*
author: Ines Delacroix, Orbital Parking Desk
seoTitle: SpaceX Catches Rocket, Solves Parallel Parking
seoDescription: Satire: SpaceX caught its Starship booster with giant mechanical chopsticks a day after missing, proving space travel's hardest part is parallel parking.
sourceEvent: SpaceX recaptured its Starship booster mid-air for the first time on Sunday, catching the returning vehicle in the launch tower's giant mechanical 'chopstick' arms a day after an earlier attempt was aborted. Previous reusable boosters landed on heavy legs and were not fully reusable, making the catch a milestone toward full reusability.

social.x: SpaceX just parallel-parked a 20-storey skyscraper into the world's most aggressive cutlery drawer — a day after mounting the kerb. Scientists confirm the hardest part of space travel was always the parking.
social.facebook: SpaceX's Starship booster returned from space on Sunday and reversed itself into a parking bay roughly the width of a dinner fork, where it was caught by two giant mechanical arms. altHeadlines: Local Rocket Successfully Reverses Into Launch Tower; No Bollards Harmed
SpaceX Booster Signals, Checks Mirrors, Parallel Parks Into Giant Chopsticks

body:
BOCA CHICA, Texas — SpaceX made aerospace history on Sunday when its returning Starship booster — a stainless-steel tower block travelling at several hundred kilometres an hour — was caught mid-air by the launch tower's giant mechanical arms, confirming what engineers have privately suspected for decades: the hardest part of space travel was always going to be parallel parking.

The capture came one day after an earlier attempt was called off, a manoeuvre one engineer described as 'mounting the kerb, stalling, and going around the block for another go'. Officials stressed the abort was 'part of the plan', in the same way that clipping the wing mirror of a parked hatchback is part of the plan.

The tower, officially named 'Mechazilla' and referred to on-site as 'the big chopsticks', closed its arms around the 71-metre vehicle as it descended — a parking space roughly the width of a dinner fork, with no reversing camera.

'From a technical standpoint, this is reversing a building into a bay while the bay applauds,' a SpaceX spokesperson said, declining to be named while still holding a small foam scorecard reading 9.5. 'Yesterday we clipped the cone. Today we parked it. Tomorrow we will do it one-handed while eating a burrito, like everyone else on the motorway.'

Witnesses reported the booster signalled its intention to merge for several minutes, checked its mirrors — technically, the entire Gulf of Mexico — and eased into place with what one observer called 'the quiet confidence of a man who has only ever driven automatics'.

Local man Derek Hollis, 51, who watched the livestream forty-seven times, described the moment as 'better than my wedding'. 'My wife agrees,' he added. 'She was at the wedding.'

The aerospace industry responded swiftly. NASA announced it was 'reviewing its own parking procedures', while the European Space Agency conceded that its rockets still 'mostly abandon themselves in the ocean like shopping trolleys'. One analyst noted that previous reusable boosters required heavy landing legs — 'the rocket equivalent of parking on someone's lawn with the handbrake off'.

SpaceX confirmed the next test would require the booster to reverse around a corner, execute a three-point turn in low Earth orbit, and park between two rival rockets on a slight incline 'within eighteen months, or whenever the examiner stops crying'.

Driving instructors have already claimed partial credit. 'We always said it was the hardest skill,' said one, who requested anonymity because his pupil was still on the roundabout.

At press time, the booster was seen edging forward three centimetres to let a smaller rocket get out.
